title: Counting events in a time window
objectives: Design a sliding-window counter and a rate limiter for timestamped events.

screens.title: Which requests get in
screens.prose: You wrote a one-client limiter in `ds` l11. A request at time $t$ counts the accepted times greater than $t - w$. Here the limit is 2 and the window is 10. New here: many clients, and a bucket.
screens.question: Three separate requests arrive, at 14, at 15 and at 16, each judged against this log. Which are accepted?

options.text: The ones at 15 and 16
Only the one at 16
options.why: You kept the time 5 in the window at 15. The cut-off is 5, and 5 is not above 5.

options.text: All three
options.why: You ignored the log. At 14 both times count, and the limit is 2.

options.text: None of them
options.why: You never forgot an old time. The window slides, so entries leave it.

hints.text: What is the cut-off for each request?
It is $t - 10$: the cut-off is 4 at 14, 5 at 15 and 6 at 16.
Count the logged times above the cut-off. At 14 that is 2. At 15 it is 1. At 16 it is 0.

feedback.correct: Only 14 is refused: at 15 and 16 the log has room.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each logged time with the cut-off $t - 10$.

byKey.b: At 15 the time 5 is not above the cut-off 5, so only 6 counts.
byKey.c: At 14 the times 5 and 6 are both above 4, so the log is full.
byKey.d: At 15 the time 5 has left the window, so there is room.

explain.text: A time counts only if it is greater than $t - 10$. At 14 the cut-off is 4, so both entries count and the request is refused. At 15 only 6 counts and at 16 none do.

widget.label: Time
widget.accept: 16: at 16 the cut-off is 6, and 6 is not above 6

hints.text: When is the cut-off equal to 6?
The cut-off is $t - 10$.
At $t = 16$ the cut-off is 6. The time 6 is not above it, so it no longer counts.

feedback.correct: At 16: the cut-off is 6, and the log needs times above it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first $t$ with $t - 10 \ge 6$.

byKey.late: You waited one second too long. At 16 the cut-off is already 6.
byKey.early: At 15 the cut-off is 5. That drops the time 5, not 6.
byKey.own: 6 is the time of the entry. Ask when it leaves.

explain.text: An entry at time $s$ counts while $s > t - 10$. It leaves when $t - 10 \ge s$, that is when $t \ge s + 10$. For $s = 6$ that is $t = 16$.

screens.title: Many clients
screens.prose: Extend the single-client log of `ds` l11: keep one deque of accepted times for each user, in a dict. Drop the old times from the left before you count.

lines: allow(user, t): True if the request is accepted.
t never goes back. Count the accepted requests of this user at times greater than t - window.
Accepted when that count is below limit.
A refused request is not recorded.
Hidden driver run_limiter(limit, window, calls): rows [user, t]. It returns the accept flags.

hints.text: What does each user need?
A deque of the times of their accepted requests.
Pop from the left while `q[0] <= t - window`. Accept and append only if `len(q) < limit`.

feedback.correct: A dict of deques, trimmed on every call.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: at time 10 the times 1, 2 and 3 are all above 0, so the request is refused.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has two users. Each user has their own log.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has window 1: a request at 1 forgets one at 0.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has limit 2, window 3: the request at 3 forgets the one at 0.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 refuses three in a row, then admits three more as the old ones age out.

explain.text: Each call pops the old times, then compares the length with the limit. Each time is added once and removed once, so a call costs constant time on average. A refused request leaves the log alone.

screens.title: Refused requests
screens.prose: Limit 2, window 10. A client sends requests at 0, 1, 5, 10 and 11. One learner appends each time to the log before checking the count.
screens.question: Which requests does a correct limiter accept?

options.text: 0 and 1 only
options.why: You recorded the refused request at 5. It stays in the log and still counts at 10 and 11.
You kept the time 1 in the window at 11. The cut-off is 1, and 1 is not above 1.

options.text: All five
options.why: The request at 5 meets a full log of two. It is refused.

hints.text: Is the request at 5 accepted?
No: the log holds 0 and 1, and the limit is 2.
Refused, so it is not recorded. At 10 the time 0 has left, so there is room. At 11 the time 1 has left.

feedback.correct: T, T, F, T, T: a refused request leaves no mark.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide each request before recording anything.

byKey.b: That is the learner's bug: a refused time sits in the log and locks the client out.
byKey.c: At 11 the cut-off is 1, so the time 1 has left and there is room.
byKey.d: The limit is 2. The third request in the window is refused.

explain.text: The request at 5 is refused and not recorded. At 10 the time 0 has left, so 10 is accepted, and at 11 the time 1 has left. Recording refused requests would keep a client locked out for as long as it keeps trying.

screens.title: A block boundary
screens.prose: A fixed counter allows 40 requests in each 30-second block and resets at each block start. 40 requests arrive at second 29, and 40 more at second 30.
screens.question: How many does the fixed counter admit?

widget.label: Requests
widget.accept: 80: 40 in each block. A sliding log would admit 40

hints.text: Which block is each request in?
Second 29 ends the first block. Second 30 starts the second.
Each block has its own count of 40, so both groups pass: 80 in two seconds.

feedback.correct: 80 in two seconds, double the limit. A sliding log admits 40.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The counter resets at second 30.

byKey.sliding: That is the sliding log's answer. A fixed counter resets at the block boundary and admits both groups.

explain.text: The two groups sit in different blocks, so each meets a fresh count and all 80 pass. A sliding log at second 30 still sees the 40 from second 29, so it admits only 40.

screens.title: A bucket of tokens
screens.prose: A token bucket allows a burst of up to `capacity`, then a steady `rate` a second. It stores two numbers, the tokens and the time of the last request, and never a list.

params.title: TokenBucket(capacity, rate)
lines: allow(t): True if the request is accepted.
The bucket starts full at time 0.
Each whole second adds rate tokens, never above capacity.
First add the tokens for the time since the last request. Then spend 1 token if there is one, else refuse.
Hidden driver run_bucket(capacity, rate, times) returns the accept flags.

hints.text: What does the bucket remember?
How many tokens it has, and when it last looked.
On a request at $t$: `tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (t - last) * rate)`. Set `last = t`. Spend one token if there is one.

feedback.correct: Two numbers: tokens and last time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: four requests at time 0 drain a bucket of 3. One token is back at each of times 1 and 2.
byKey.test-2: Test 2: capacity 2, rate 2: two tokens at time 0, two more at time 1.

explain.text: The bucket refills lazily: each request adds the tokens for the time that has passed, capped at the capacity. Spending a token is one subtraction. Memory stays at two numbers however many requests arrive.

screens.title: Log and bucket
screens.prose:
Two shapes, one idea: forget what is old.

```python
# sliding log
while q and q[0] <= t - window:
    q.popleft()
if len(q) < limit: q.append(t)

# token bucket
tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (t - last) * rate)
```
screens.question: Put the steps of the sliding log's `allow` in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Take the user's deque, or make an empty one
Drop times at or before `t - window` from the left
If fewer than `limit` remain, append `t` and accept
Otherwise refuse and leave the log alone
Append `t`, then count the times inside the window
lines.why: A refused request would sit in the log and count against the client's next requests.

hints.text: What must happen before you count?
The old times must be dropped.
Get the log, drop the old times, test the count, then accept with a record or refuse without one.

feedback.correct: Drop the old, then test, then record only if accepted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only after old times are gone.

byKey.d1: You recorded before deciding. A refused request must leave no mark.
byKey.left-out: Four steps belong. Only record-first is wrong.

explain.text: The log forgets old times from the left, then compares the count with the limit. The bucket forgets by adding tokens for the time passed. Both decide first and record only an accepted request.

screens.title: A million clients
screens.prose: A gateway serves a million clients. Each sends one request and never returns. The limiter keeps a deque for every client it has ever seen.
screens.question: What do you change?

options.text: Delete an entry when its deque empties, and sweep idle clients.
Keep every client for ever, so that no request history is lost.
options.why: You let memory grow with every client ever seen. An old client's log is useless.

options.text: Raise `limit` so that fewer deques are needed overall.
options.why: The limit does not change how many clients there are.

options.text: Use one shared deque for all clients to save the memory.
options.why: One log would count a client's requests against everyone else.

hints.text: What does an idle client's entry hold?
Times that have left the window, so nothing useful.
Drop an entry once its deque is empty. A timer sweep catches clients that never call again.

feedback.correct: Free the entries that hold nothing live.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what memory is wasted.

byKey.b: History older than the window never matters again.
byKey.c: The number of deques is the number of clients, not the limit.
byKey.d: A shared log breaks the limit for each client.

explain.text: Once every time in a deque has left the window, the entry carries no information. Deleting it frees memory for the next client. A sweep matters because a client that never returns is never visited.

screens.title: Which limiter
screens.prose: Match each need to a limiter. (a) A hard cap of 100 a minute at an exchange gateway. (b) Bursts allowed, but a steady average. (c) A cheap counter that may be a little off.
screens.question: Which match is right?

options.text: (a) sliding log, (b) token bucket, (c) fixed window
(a) fixed window, (b) sliding log, (c) token bucket
options.why: You gave the hard cap to the fixed window. Around a boundary it lets twice the limit through.

options.text: (a) token bucket, (b) fixed window, (c) sliding log
options.why: You gave the hard cap to a bucket, which allows a burst up to its capacity. The log stores every request, so it is not cheap.

options.text: (a) sliding log, (b) fixed window, (c) token bucket
options.why: You gave bursts to the fixed window. A bucket is built for them.

hints.text: Which limiter never exceeds the limit in any window?
The sliding log. It stores a time for each accepted request.
The bucket allows bursts and bounds the average. The fixed window is a single counter with boundary error.

feedback.correct: Log for the hard cap, bucket for bursts, fixed window for cheap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match accuracy, burst and memory to each need.

byKey.b: Fixed windows are cheap but inexact at a boundary.
byKey.c: A bucket is not a hard cap, and the log is the dearest in memory.
byKey.d: A fixed window gives bursts only by accident, at a boundary.

explain.text: A sliding log is exact but stores a time per request. A token bucket stores two numbers and allows a burst up to its capacity. A fixed window is the cheapest, and it can admit twice the limit around a boundary.

ideas: A sliding log keeps each client's accepted times in a deque. It drops those at or before $t - w$ and accepts if fewer than the limit remain.
A refused request is never recorded. A client's entry can be freed once its deque is empty.
A token bucket stores a token count and a last time. It adds tokens for the time passed and spends one per request.
